claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by a balance between bulk configurational entropy and surface-segregation energetics.
The initial nanoparticles are five-component or higher solid solutions with near-equal atomic ratios and homogeneous elemental distributions.
Thermal annealing across 473–1923 K activates atomic diffusion.
High-temperature annealing induces surface segregation in the Pd-Cu-Pt-Ni-Co HEA system.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation sufficiently that observed changes can be attributed solely to temperature-driven atomic dynamics.
Cu and Pd preferentially enrich at the nanoparticle surface during annealing.
Co, Ni, and Pt are preferentially retained in the bulk relative to Cu and Pd.
The relatively low cohesive contribution associated with Cu's filled d-band favors Cu surface segregation.
Pd's cohesive and surface energies, which are only marginally higher than those of Cu, contribute to Pd surface segregation.
Migration of Cu to the surface reduces the system's internal energy.
Bulk configurational entropy favors an approximately equimolar bulk distribution and opposes phase separation.
Moderate surface segregation optimizes interfacial energetics and preserves the overall solid-solution structure.
Nanoparticles with moderate Cu and Pd surface enrichment and a uniformly mixed bulk retain catalytic performance across the stated temperature range.
Nanoparticles with moderate Cu and Pd surface enrichment and a uniformly mixed bulk retain thermoelectric performance across the stated temperature range.
Samples exhibiting no segregation will perform worse than samples exhibiting moderate segregation.
Excessive segregation leads to phase separation and diminished catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Excessively long or hot annealing can produce complete phase separation, while insufficient annealing produces no segregation.
